rules.title: El punto desde el que miras
rules.text: El tiempo verbal expresa tu perspectiva. Past simple sitúa un hecho en un periodo terminado; present perfect conecta el pasado con una situación actual. Present perfect continuous destaca una actividad y su duración, sin asegurar que haya terminado. Compara un informe acabado con el trabajo que te ha tenido ocupado. Los verbos de estado, como know u own, normalmente no usan forma continua en ese sentido. Una duración no obliga al continuo: puedes decir I have known her for years. Primero decide qué quieres comunicar y después elige la forma.
rules.pattern: finished time → past simple; current result → have + participle; ongoing activity → have been + -ing
rules.tip: No combines present perfect con yesterday si ese adverbio sitúa el hecho terminado.
examples: I have been working on this report all morning, and it is still unfinished.
We published the results last Friday.
I have known my mentor for several years.

rules.title: Una historia tiene capas
rules.text: Past simple lleva los acontecimientos principales. Past continuous presenta el fondo o una actividad en marcha. Past perfect marca un hecho anterior a otro momento pasado; no hace falta mantenerlo cuando el orden ya está claro. Past perfect continuous añade duración anterior y puede explicar un resultado visible. En una narración, evita saltar de tiempo sin cambiar el punto de referencia. Dibuja una línea temporal de tres hechos, cuenta primero la escena y revela después lo que había pasado antes.
rules.pattern: was/were + -ing; had + participle; had been + -ing
rules.tip: No uses past perfect solo porque un hecho ocurrió hace mucho tiempo.
examples: When I reached the station, the train had already left.
They were exhausted because they had been walking for hours before they found shelter.
I was checking the map when the battery died.

rules.title: Hábitos que ya no son iguales
rules.text: Used to sirve para hábitos y estados pasados que contrastan con el presente. Would puede contar acciones repetidas cuando el periodo pasado está establecido, pero normalmente no estados como own o believe. Be used to significa estar acostumbrado; get used to describe el proceso de adaptación. En estas dos estructuras to es preposición: detrás va un nombre o -ing. Cuenta un cambio real, explica qué costó y cómo te adaptaste; así practicas significado y forma juntos.
rules.pattern: used to + base; be/get used to + noun/-ing
rules.tip: Did you use to…? y I did not use to… llevan use, sin -d.

units.story:
When Mara moved to another city, she expected her English to improve simply because she would hear it every day. She had studied grammar for years and could explain several complicated rules. Yet her first week at a community workshop was uncomfortable. While other volunteers were discussing the schedule, she was silently translating each sentence. By the time she had prepared a reply, the conversation had moved on.

The organiser suggested a smaller goal: ask one useful question at every meeting and report one decision afterwards. Mara began keeping a notebook, but she did not fill it with isolated words. Instead, she recorded expressions she had needed, such as asking someone to clarify a deadline. The next week she deliberately used those expressions in a different situation.

Three months later, Mara still occasionally misses a joke. However, she has become much better at noticing when she needs clarification. She has been helping new volunteers this month, which gives her a reason to explain procedures without reading. She used to judge a conversation by the number of mistakes she made. Now she also asks whether the people involved understood each other and completed their task. Her progress has not been a straight line, but it has become easier to recognise.

units.case:
At an evening class, two learners compared their study records. Joel had completed ninety short exercises in one weekend. Lina had completed fewer, but she could describe three situations in which she had reused the language. Joel felt disappointed until their tutor asked him to tell a story about a missed train. He knew the vocabulary, yet he kept changing between present and past without a reason.

They tried the task again with three notes: background, interruption and earlier cause. This time, Joel explained that he had been looking at the wrong platform while an announcement was being made. Lina listened and asked what he had done next. Her unexpected question made him retrieve the language rather than repeat a script.

A week later, both learners told a new story without the notes. Joel still hesitated, but his listener could follow the events. They agreed to keep the exercise totals in their records while adding a second measure: something they could now do outside the exercise. Neither learner treated one good performance as proof that the skill would always be available.

units.model:
When I joined a community garden, I assumed that understanding the instructions would be enough. I had studied English at school, but I had rarely used it while doing a practical task. During my first session, I kept agreeing even when I was unsure what people meant. As a result, I planted several seedlings in the wrong place.

Since then, I have been trying a different approach. I repeat the important part of an instruction in my own words and ask whether I have understood correctly. At first, I felt that this would annoy the other volunteers. In fact, it has prevented several misunderstandings and helped us work together.

My advice is to choose one small communication goal for each session. You could ask a follow-up question or explain a procedure to someone new. Keep a note of what worked, then try it again in another situation. Progress becomes more visible when you notice what you can actually do.

units.title: Planes, previsiones y plazos
units.goal: Explicar previsiones y compromisos, negociar plazos y distinguir procesos futuros de resultados completados.

rules.title: Elegir una forma de futuro
rules.text: Will puede expresar una decisión al hablar, una promesa o una predicción. Going to suele presentar una intención previa o una predicción basada en evidencia actual. Present continuous puede presentar un acuerdo concreto; present simple sirve para horarios. Estas formas se solapan según el contexto: una palabra como tomorrow no determina por sí sola la elección. Al planificar, aclara qué está decidido, qué depende de otras personas y qué solo es una posibilidad. Practica una conversación en la que alguien cambia el plan y debes responder.
rules.pattern: decision now: will; intention/evidence: going to; arrangement: present continuous
rules.tip: Una previsión no se convierte en compromiso solo porque uses will.
examples: The train leaves at seven according to the timetable.
Those boxes are unstable. They are going to fall.
I am meeting the designer on Thursday; we have already agreed on the time.

rules.title: Estar haciendo frente a haber terminado
rules.text: Future continuous coloca una actividad en desarrollo en un momento futuro. Future perfect mira hacia atrás desde un punto futuro y presenta algo ya terminado. By significa como máximo para ese momento; until marca continuidad hasta un límite. Future perfect continuous añade duración hasta ese punto, sobre todo con actividades. Elige primero una fecha de referencia y después pregunta: ¿la tarea estará en marcha, completada o habrá durado cierto tiempo? No conviertas todas las fechas límite en until.
rules.pattern: will be + -ing; will have + participle; will have been + -ing
rules.tip: By Friday y until Friday expresan relaciones temporales diferentes.
examples: By Friday, we will have completed the first stage.
At ten tomorrow, I will be presenting the proposal.
By June, we will have been working together for a year.

rules.title: Condiciones y calendarios realistas
rules.text: En una cláusula temporal que se refiere al futuro, after, before, once, when y as soon as suelen llevar presente, no will. El present perfect puede destacar que una acción estará completada antes de la siguiente. Unless significa if not; provided that introduce una condición necesaria. In case suele presentar una precaución ante una posibilidad y no equivale simplemente a if. Para negociar un plazo, combina un compromiso limitado, una condición y un plan alternativo.
rules.pattern: once/as soon as + present; main clause + future
rules.tip: I will call when I arrive, sin will después de when en esta cláusula temporal.
examples: We will send the invitation once everyone has confirmed.
Take a printed copy in case the network fails.
We can finish by Monday provided that the materials arrive on time.

units.story:
A student association decided to organise a skills fair. At the first meeting, everyone spoke confidently about what would happen, but the calendar soon revealed a problem: three people had promised the same room to different speakers. The organiser, Nia, asked the team to separate intentions from confirmed arrangements.

They created three columns. One contained bookings that had already been agreed. Another contained tasks they expected to finish by a particular date. The third listed events that depended on something else. By the end of the week, they would have contacted every speaker, but they would not publish the programme until the room bookings were confirmed.

One volunteer proposed printing hundreds of programmes immediately to save money. Another pointed out that a cheap early order could become expensive if the schedule changed. They decided to print a small number and display a digital version that could be updated. A paper notice would remain available in case the network failed.

The fair eventually started fifteen minutes late because a visiting speaker missed a train. This was inconvenient, but it did not destroy the day. The team used a prepared discussion activity while they waited. Their plan had become useful precisely because it included uncertainty rather than hiding it behind confident predictions.

units.case:
A neighbourhood library plans to open on Sunday mornings for a six-week trial. Volunteers have offered to help, but the librarian refuses to announce permanent opening hours yet. By the final week, the library will have collected attendance figures and comments from visitors. During the trial, staff will be comparing the demand with the cost of keeping the building open.

Several residents would like a decision immediately. The librarian explains that making a promise before evaluating the trial could lead to a sudden closure later. Instead, the notice gives a clear review date and states which services will be available. Book borrowing will continue as usual, whereas technical support will depend on a specialist being present.

The plan includes a practical precaution: if fewer than two volunteers can attend, the session will be cancelled and a notice will be posted the previous evening. This condition is visible before anyone registers. Residents may dislike the uncertainty, but they can make better plans when it is expressed honestly.

Hi everyone,

I am writing to confirm the arrangements for our photography workshop. We have booked the community hall for Saturday, and two local photographers have agreed to lead the practical sessions. Participants will arrive at ten, while the organising team will be setting up from nine.

By Thursday, we will have received the final list of equipment. Please let me know before then if you can lend us a tripod. We expect most people to bring a phone, so the activities will not require an expensive camera.

We are planning a short walk after lunch, provided that the weather is suitable. If it rains, we will practise indoor portraits instead. Please bring a light jacket in case the temperature changes during the walk.

I will send the group list as soon as everyone has confirmed. Could you check these arrangements and tell me if I have missed anything? It would be useful to resolve any problems before Friday.

Best wishes,
Rosa

units.title: Decisiones y alternativas
units.goal: Analizar decisiones pasadas y sus consecuencias actuales sin confundir hechos con hipótesis.

rules.title: Un pasado que no ocurrió
rules.text: Third conditional imagina una condición pasada diferente y su resultado pasado. La realidad se deduce del contexto: If we had left earlier sugiere que no salimos antes. Had + participle va en la condición; would have + participle expresa el resultado imaginado. Could have añade posibilidad o capacidad; might have expresa un resultado menos seguro. Antes de formar la frase, escribe dos hechos reales y luego cambia uno mentalmente. La contracción had y would puede sonar igual, pero su posición y el verbo siguiente aclaran su función.
rules.pattern: if + had + participle → would/could/might have + participle
rules.tip: En este patrón evita would have en la cláusula con if.
examples: If we had checked the address, we would have found the building.
She would have attended if she had received the invitation.
Without your advice, I might have made the same mistake.

rules.title: Cuando el resultado llega hasta hoy
rules.text: Un mixed conditional puede unir una condición pasada irreal con un resultado presente: una decisión anterior explica una situación imaginada ahora. También puede unir una característica presente con una consecuencia pasada. Las formas no se eligen por una receta única; se eligen según el momento de cada idea. Añade now o yesterday cuando ayuden al interlocutor, pero no dependas solo de esas palabras. Explica primero la realidad y después la alternativa para que no parezca que estás afirmando algo que ocurrió.
rules.pattern: past cause → if + had done, would be now; present trait → if + past, would have done
rules.tip: Identifica por separado el tiempo de la condición y el del resultado.
examples: If I had accepted that job, I would live abroad now.
If I were more confident, I would have spoken at yesterday's meeting.
If they had repaired the bridge, the road would be open now.

rules.title: Alternativas con límites y matices
rules.text: Unless introduce una condición negativa. Provided that, as long as y on condition that presentan límites o requisitos. Even if indica que el resultado se mantiene a pesar de una posibilidad. Supposing invita a explorar una hipótesis. Al discutir una decisión, compara opciones y consecuencias en vez de formar frases aisladas: qué se habría evitado, qué sigue siendo incierto y qué harías de otra manera. Una hipótesis razonable debe respetar los hechos conocidos y no presentar una predicción como certeza.
rules.pattern: unless = if not; even if = aunque ocurra; provided that = siempre que
rules.tip: Unless no suele combinarse con otra negación para el mismo sentido.
examples: We can use the hall provided that we leave it clean.
Even if the price falls, we will not buy it because we do not need it.

units.story:
A small theatre had to choose between repairing its old lights and hiring new equipment for one season. The director preferred hiring because it required less money immediately. A technician warned that the company would still need a permanent solution later, but the first performance was approaching and the decision was made quickly.

The hired lights worked well. However, when the following season began, prices had risen and the theatre could no longer afford the same arrangement. Some volunteers argued that repairing the original equipment would certainly have solved everything. The technician disagreed with that certainty: the old lights might have needed further repairs, and the earlier inspection had not covered every part.

At a review meeting, the team separated what they knew from what they could only imagine. If they had requested a detailed inspection, they would have had better information. That did not prove that repairing was the best choice, but it revealed a weakness in the decision process. They agreed that future decisions would include an estimate of costs over several seasons, even if a short-term option initially looked attractive. The discussion became more useful when the question changed from who was to blame to what information they had failed to obtain.

Leo declined an exchange programme because he assumed his application would be unsuccessful. Months later, a friend explained that the organisers also considered motivation and practical experience. Leo realised he had rejected himself before anyone else could assess him.

He cannot know whether he would have been accepted. Saying that he would certainly be living abroad now would ignore that uncertainty. He can, however, identify a different decision he could have made: ask for information and apply. If he had applied, he might at least have gained experience of the process.

For the next opportunity, Leo plans to list the evidence for each concern. A genuine financial obstacle needs a different response from a fear based on an assumption. He will apply provided that the travel costs are covered. Even if he is not selected, he expects the experience to help him prepare a stronger application later.

units.title: Deseos, preferencias y arrepentimientos
units.goal: Expresar deseos y desacuerdos con tacto, y convertir un arrepentimiento en una acción concreta.

rules.title: Desear un presente distinto
rules.text: Wish + past simple expresa que te gustaría una situación presente diferente. Con be, were se usa con todos los sujetos en estilo hipotético; was también aparece en contextos menos formales. Wish + could expresa capacidad o posibilidad deseada. No interpretes el pasado de esta estructura como una fecha anterior: señala distancia respecto de la realidad. Para un futuro que consideras posible, hope suele ser más apropiado. Explica qué situación real te gustaría cambiar antes de practicar la estructura.
rules.pattern: wish + past; wish + could; hope + present/future
rules.tip: I hope you enjoy it expresa una esperanza posible; no I wish you enjoy it.
examples: I wish I had more time to practise today.

rules.title: Mirar atrás sin quedarse allí
rules.text: Wish + past perfect presenta un arrepentimiento sobre algo pasado. If only puede expresar un deseo más intenso y también usa pasado o past perfect según el momento. Should have + participle evalúa lo que habría sido mejor hacer; no afirma que se hiciera. Relaciona cada arrepentimiento con una medida concreta: pedir detalles, confirmar un horario o empezar antes. Así la práctica consiste en explicar una experiencia y aprender de ella, no en repetir lamentos sin contexto.
rules.pattern: wish/if only + had + participle; should have + participle
rules.tip: I wish I had asked significa que no pregunté y ahora lo lamento.

rules.title: Quejas y preferencias con tacto

It is time + sujeto + pasado señala que algo debería hacerse ya. El tono importa: describe el efecto de la conducta y formula una petición clara, no una acusación general.
rules.pattern: would rather do; would rather someone did; it is time someone did
rules.tip: Después de would rather, la misma persona usa base verbal, sin to.
examples: I would rather discuss this in person.

It is time we reviewed the way we share information.

units.story:
Two flatmates, Ana and Ben, had avoided discussing the noise in their shared kitchen. Ana worked early and wished the apartment were quieter at night. Ben studied late and assumed that the walls were thick enough to prevent anyone being disturbed. Both were becoming frustrated, yet neither knew the other's routine in detail.

One evening, Ana said, "I wish you would stop making so much noise." Ben heard this as criticism of his whole lifestyle. The conversation became less productive until Ana explained the specific problem: she could hear cupboard doors closing after midnight. Ben said he wished she had mentioned it earlier, because he could easily have prepared his food before studying.

They agreed on a trial arrangement rather than a permanent rule immediately. Ben would prepare what he needed before ten, and Ana would tell him if the noise continued. Ana also acknowledged that she had sometimes played music early in the morning without considering Ben's sleep.

The agreement did not require either person to become completely silent. It required each to describe a need, understand its effect on the other and test a practical change. A week later, they reviewed the arrangement and adjusted one detail. Their first uncomfortable conversation had become the start of a workable habit.

units.case:
A club member regretted not challenging an unrealistic deadline. At the time, everyone sounded confident, and she did not want to appear negative. When the project ran late, she wrote that she wished she had spoken up.

Her mentor asked her to turn that sentence into a future action. Instead of promising to be braver in general, she prepared two questions: what evidence supported the estimate, and which task could be reduced if time became short? At the next meeting, these questions led to a calmer discussion than a direct claim that the plan was impossible.

The member still preferred to think before speaking. She did not need to become a different person. She needed a useful way to contribute while the decision was still open. Looking back helped because it changed what she did next.

Cannot have o could not have expresan que algo parece incompatible con las pruebas. El grado de seguridad depende de la evidencia, no de que el verbo suene más avanzado. Describe primero el indicio y luego tu conclusión. Si hay otra explicación compatible, reconoce ese límite.
rules.pattern: must/might/cannot have + participle
rules.tip: Must not have puede expresar una deducción negativa en algunos usos; para imposibilidad, practica cannot have.
examples: The floor is wet. Someone must have spilled some water.
She was abroad that day, so she cannot have attended the meeting in person.
They might have misunderstood the room number.

rules.title: Consejo y necesidad pasados
rules.text: Should have expresa una acción recomendable que normalmente no se hizo; should not have evalúa una acción inconveniente. Need not have + participle indica que se hizo algo innecesario. Did not need to expresa ausencia de necesidad y, sin contexto adicional, no asegura por sí solo si se hizo o no. Compara relatos concretos para distinguir hechos de evaluaciones retrospectivas. Evita convertir una crítica en una afirmación de culpa sin conocer las circunstancias.
rules.pattern: should have done; need not have done; did not need to do
rules.tip: Need not have bought indica que sí se compró.
examples: I bought a ticket, but entry was free. I need not have bought one.

I did not need to take a taxi because the last bus was still running.

rules.title: Capacidad y oportunidades

units.story:
A box of donated books disappeared from the entrance of a community centre. One volunteer immediately assumed that somebody had taken it without permission. Another noticed that the label was wet and suggested that a cleaner might have moved the box away from a leak. Neither person had actually seen what happened.

The coordinator asked them to record observations separately from explanations. A photograph showed the box beside the door at nine. A delivery driver remembered seeing it later, but could not give an exact time. The cleaner confirmed that she had moved several boxes, although she did not remember their contents.

Eventually, they found the books in a storage room. The box had been placed there to keep the entrance clear during a delivery. The volunteer who moved it had left a note, but the note had fallen behind a chair. The coordinator did not treat this as evidence that notes were useless. Instead, the team agreed on one visible place for messages about moved items. Their investigation worked because they checked possible explanations before turning the first suspicion into an accusation.

units.case:
After a group missed a reservation, several people said that the organiser must have forgotten to book. The organiser showed the confirmation email, which ruled out that explanation. The group then noticed that the confirmation listed a different date.

It was possible that the wrong date had been entered, but the booking history showed that the venue had changed it while transferring reservations to a new system. The venue apologised and offered another session. The organiser still felt that she should have checked the updated confirmation instead of assuming it was identical to the first.

Two statements could therefore be true: she had made the original booking correctly, and an additional check might have prevented the wasted journey. Discussing both facts helped the group improve its routine without inventing a simple story in which one person had caused every problem.

rules.title: Elegir el foco de la información
rules.text: La pasiva permite empezar por la persona o cosa afectada. Conserva el tiempo en be y usa el participio del verbo principal. El agente con by se añade si aporta información; no se inventa cuando se desconoce. Una pasiva no es automáticamente más formal ni mejor: decide qué necesita saber tu lector primero. Compara una instrucción, un aviso y una noticia para observar cómo cambia el foco.

rules.tip: Is being repaired indica un proceso en curso; has been repaired indica un resultado.

units.story:
When a community centre replaced its booking system, staff expected fewer mistakes. Instead, several reservations disappeared during the first week. The manager initially described the change as a technical failure, but an inspection showed that the software had saved the entries correctly. The problem occurred when information was copied between two separate lists.

The centre had hired a company to install the system, but had not arranged training for everyone who would use it. One receptionist assumed that cancelling an old entry was necessary before moving it to the new calendar. Another entered the same booking twice because she had not been told how to check its status.

Rather than buying another system immediately, the manager had the workflow reviewed. A short procedure was written, and staff practised using fictional bookings before returning to live ones. Every reservation was then assigned a visible status, and changes were recorded in one place.

The revised process did not remove the need for judgement. Unusual requests still had to be discussed. However, routine tasks became easier to follow, and staff could explain to visitors what had been confirmed and what was still being checked. The improvement came from coordinating people and information, not simply installing newer technology.

A cycling club offered a free inspection day. The notice said that bicycles would be checked, but several visitors assumed that every repair would also be completed without charge. The volunteers had to explain that an inspection identified problems; it did not include unlimited parts or labour.

For the next event, the club changed the notice. It listed what would be inspected, which minor adjustments were included and when a separate estimate would be needed. Visitors were asked to describe the problem before leaving their bicycles.

The clearer description helped both sides. Volunteers could allocate time realistically, while owners could decide whether to have further work done. A service became easier to evaluate when its limits were made visible.

units.title: Transmitir mensajes con precisión
units.goal: Transmitir afirmaciones, preguntas y peticiones sin cambiar su intención ni confundir la fuente.

rules.title: Cambiar el punto de vista
rules.text: Reported speech adapta un mensaje a otro hablante, momento o lugar. Con un verbo de reporte pasado, a menudo se retrocede un tiempo verbal, pero no es obligatorio si el contenido sigue vigente y eliges presentarlo así. Pronombres y expresiones como here o tomorrow cambian solo cuando cambia la referencia real. No sustituyas palabras mecánicamente: identifica quién habló, a quién se refería y qué información sigue siendo cierta.
rules.pattern: said (that) + clause; told + person + clause
rules.tip: Say no lleva objeto personal directo: she told me / she said to me.
examples: She told me she had finished the draft the previous day.
He said that the office was closed.
The teacher said that water freezes at zero degrees Celsius under standard conditions.

rules.title: Preguntas e instrucciones indirectas
rules.text: Las preguntas indirectas usan orden afirmativo: sujeto antes del verbo. If o whether introducen preguntas de sí/no; las preguntas con what, where y otros interrogativos conservan esa palabra. Al transmitir una instrucción, usa ask/tell someone to do; una prohibición emplea not to. El signo de pregunta pertenece a la frase global si realmente estás preguntando: Could you tell me where it is? no invierte it is.
rules.pattern: asked where + subject + verb; asked if/whether; told someone (not) to
rules.tip: No conserves do/did como auxiliar interrogativo dentro de la pregunta indirecta.
examples: She asked where the nearest station was.
They told us not to enter the room.
Could you tell me whether the fee includes materials?

rules.title: Verbos que expresan la intención
rules.text: Reporting verbs añaden intención: promise/offer/refuse + to; admit/deny/suggest + -ing; remind/warn/encourage + persona + to. Otros patrones llevan preposición: apologise for, insist on, accuse someone of. Una elección incorrecta puede cambiar el sentido: suggested no equivale a insisted. Lee un diálogo, identifica si propone, obliga, reconoce o rechaza y después resume con el patrón adecuado.
rules.pattern: offer to; admit doing; remind someone to; apologise for doing
rules.tip: Suggest doing o suggest that we do; evita suggest me to do.
examples: He admitted losing the key.
She reminded me to check the date.
They suggested postponing the discussion until everyone could attend.

A notice in a student group announced that a local museum would offer free entry to everyone on Friday. Dozens of people shared the message. When the museum received calls, staff explained that free entry had only been offered to registered participants in a particular workshop.

The group administrator posted a correction and linked to the booking information. Rather than quietly deleting the first notice, she explained exactly which part had been inaccurate. She also asked members to check whether a summary preserved restrictions, dates and the identity of the source.

units.story:
A walking tour of a historic district had become difficult for new visitors to follow. The guide described buildings with long lists of dates, owners and renovations. Participants could remember interesting details, but several could not identify which building was being discussed.

A volunteer suggested changing the order of information. Each description would begin with a visible feature that distinguished the building from its neighbours. Additional history would follow only after everyone had located the subject. Instead of starting with the architect's biography, the guide might say, "The house with the blue balcony, which was once a small school, is our next stop."

The revised tour also distinguished essential directions from optional background information. Visitors who wanted more detail could read a short booklet afterwards. People using wheelchairs were given clear information about the section reached by steps, together with an alternative route.

The guide did not remove complexity from the history itself. She made it easier to connect each fact with the right place. At the end of the tour, visitors were asked to describe one building to a partner who had not seen it. The task revealed whether their descriptions actually helped someone identify a place, rather than merely displaying how many facts they remembered.

A learner complained that she knew many expressions but could not use them in conversation. Her tutor asked how she practised. She explained that she usually read a list, covered the translations and tried to remember the meanings. This helped her recognise vocabulary, but it rarely required her to decide what to say to another person.

They designed a different task. The learner had to arrange a meeting with someone whose calendar she could not see. She could ask questions, suggest alternatives and explain a preference, but she could not read a prepared dialogue. At first, she stopped frequently to check a form. After feedback, she repeated the task with a new schedule.

The tutor did not tell her to avoid grammar. Instead, they examined the structures she had actually needed: agreeing to meet, considering changing a time and looking forward to seeing someone. The next day, she used the same patterns to organise a different activity.

The exercise was useful because the language had a purpose and the result could be checked: had they found a time that worked for both? Remembering a rule remained part of the process, but it was connected to listening, choosing and responding.

units.model:
If you find it difficult to use English in conversation, I recommend practising tasks with a clear outcome. For example, try arranging a meeting with a partner who has different free times. You will need to ask questions, consider alternatives and agree on a decision.

Before starting, choose a few useful expressions, but avoid writing every sentence you plan to say. A complete script may make the first attempt easier while preventing you from responding naturally to new information. Brief notes are usually more flexible.

After the conversation, identify one point that caused difficulty. Perhaps you forgot to ask a follow-up question or used an unclear time expression. Practise that part and then repeat the task with different details.

This approach does not mean ignoring grammar. It means studying the forms you need and putting them into practice. Remember to listen as carefully as you speak, because reaching an agreement depends on understanding the other person's information as well as expressing your own.

units.story:
A club announced that eighty per cent of its members preferred evening workshops. The statement sounded decisive until someone asked how many people had replied. Only ten of the club's sixty members had completed the survey, and eight of those ten had chosen the evening option.

The result was not invented, but its presentation encouraged a broader conclusion than the evidence supported. It described the respondents, not necessarily the entire membership. People who attended daytime sessions had been less likely to see the survey because it had been shared at an evening meeting.

The organisers sent a second invitation through several channels and left a paper copy at reception. They also asked whether transport or caring responsibilities affected people's choices. The later responses showed that some members preferred afternoons, while others could only attend online.

The club did not need a complicated statistical model to improve its decision. It needed to explain the size and limitations of its sample and avoid treating missing answers as agreement. Instead of choosing one permanent time immediately, it tested two schedules and compared attendance. A little more care with quantities changed both the wording of the announcement and the fairness of the plan.

Two teams each reported a rise in attendance. The first increased from ten to twenty people; the second increased from one hundred to one hundred and twenty. The first had the larger percentage increase, while the second added more people in absolute terms.

Neither description was false. They answered different questions. A small initial number can make a percentage change look dramatic, while an absolute increase may conceal how large the original group was.

In their joint report, the teams included both the starting and finishing numbers. Readers could then compare the changes without guessing the baseline. Clear reporting meant giving enough context for the figures to be interpreted, rather than selecting only the measure that sounded most impressive.

Most of the respondents said that a quiet environment was more important than new furniture. A few also mentioned a shortage of electrical sockets. However, there was little support for extending the opening hours late into the evening.

units.story:
A group compared two language clubs before choosing one. The first offered a large library, modern classrooms and long lectures. The second met in a smaller building and had fewer resources, but participants spent much more time solving tasks in pairs. The advertisement for each described it as the best place to improve.

Rather than accept either claim, the group listed its own priorities: opportunities to speak, feedback and a timetable compatible with work. The larger club was considerably better equipped, but equipment was not their main difficulty. They already had access to books; they needed regular interaction.

They attended one session at each club and recorded what they actually did. In the smaller club, they negotiated a plan and received feedback on a misunderstanding. In the larger one, they listened to a useful explanation but had little chance to respond.

The group chose the smaller club for that term. This did not prove that it was better for every learner. Someone preparing an individual research project might value the larger library more. Their decision was stronger because they had compared the options against a specific need instead of treating one attractive feature as evidence of overall quality.

units.story:
A school considered replacing all printed instructions with digital ones. Supporters argued that digital documents were easier to update and would reduce paper use. Critics pointed out that some students shared devices or had unreliable access to the internet outside school. Both groups had identified real concerns, but the first debate treated them as incompatible positions.

A teacher asked the students to write a paragraph that included a benefit of the other side's proposal. This did not require them to abandon their own view. It required them to explain how their preferred option would respond to a genuine limitation.

One group suggested making digital documents the default while keeping printed copies available on request. Another proposed a short trial so that the school could observe which instructions students actually used. These proposals connected purpose, evidence and practical conditions more clearly than the original slogans.

The final recommendation supported a gradual change rather than an immediate ban on paper. The students still disagreed about some costs. Nevertheless, their disagreement had become easier to discuss because they could identify the specific point at issue. Connectors helped express these relationships, but the stronger argument came from considering the relationships themselves.

Working with others can help students explain ideas, listen to different views and reach decisions together. These are skills that are difficult to practise through worksheets alone.

When a reading club began collecting unfamiliar vocabulary, its shared list quickly grew to several hundred words. Members enjoyed seeing the total increase, but many could not use the items when discussing a book. Some entries contained only one Spanish translation, even when the English expression had several meanings.

The club changed the format. Each new entry needed a short context and a phrase in which the word naturally occurred. Members also wrote a question that would invite someone else to use the expression. For example, instead of listing responsibility alone, they asked who should take responsibility for organising the next meeting.

At the following session, each person used two expressions in a fresh discussion. Others listened for meaning rather than simply checking whether the target words had appeared. If an expression sounded forced, the group discussed a more suitable context.

The vocabulary list grew more slowly after that, but it became more useful. The club had not discovered a shortcut that removed the need for repetition. It had given repetition a purpose: retrieve a phrase, adapt it to a situation and notice whether it helped communicate the intended idea.

A college debated whether attendance at public lectures should be compulsory. Supporters argued that students sometimes avoided topics outside their immediate interests, and that a shared lecture could introduce ideas they would not otherwise encounter. Opponents replied that compulsory attendance did not guarantee attention or understanding.

A student representative proposed a different approach: require learners to engage with one unfamiliar topic, but let them choose between attending a lecture, listening to a recording or interviewing a specialist.

The proposal did not remove every difficulty. Organising alternatives required time, and the quality of the follow-up task would matter. Nevertheless, it separated the educational purpose from one particular method of achieving it.

The committee agreed to test the idea with a small group. Students would submit a short explanation of what they had learned and one question they still had. Attendance remained relevant for some activities, but the new discussion asked what evidence would show meaningful engagement. A more useful argument emerged when participants clarified the purpose behind their preferred rule.

A university newsletter reported that students who attended a study group obtained higher average marks than those who did not. The headline described the group as a proven way to improve results. However, the article contained a detail that complicated this conclusion: participation had been voluntary.

Students who chose to attend might already have been more motivated or had more free time. The study had not assigned participants randomly, so it could not isolate the effect of the group from every other difference. This did not make the findings worthless. It meant that the strongest conclusion in the headline went beyond the evidence described.

A student preparing a summary initially wrote that study groups caused higher marks. After rereading the method, she changed the sentence to say that attendance was associated with higher marks in the group studied. She also retained a practical observation: participants valued the opportunity to explain difficult ideas to one another.

Her revised summary was less dramatic but more useful. It preserved both a possible benefit and a limitation. Readers could decide whether to try a study group without being told that one observational result guaranteed an improvement for everyone.

A team preparing a public exhibition kept missing internal deadlines. Members worked hard, but each interpreted "finished" differently. One considered a text finished when the first draft was written. Another assumed it had already been checked and approved. As a result, later tasks repeatedly began with incomplete material.

At the next meeting, the coordinator asked everyone to describe what they needed from the previous stage. The designer needed approved text, not a draft that might change substantially. The printer needed files in a specific format and a confirmed quantity. Volunteers needed instructions that reflected the final layout.

The team defined a small set of completion criteria and assigned one person to confirm each handover. They also reduced the number of display panels rather than pretending the original schedule remained realistic. This disappointed some members, but it made the remaining commitments more credible.

After the exhibition, the team reviewed the process. The biggest improvement had not come from asking people to work faster. It came from making expectations visible and negotiating the scope before the final week. Clear communication became part of completing a task, rather than something to do only after the practical work was over.

rules.title: Hecho, opinión y atribución
rules.text: Un hecho se puede comprobar; una opinión interpreta o evalúa. Un texto puede combinarlos en una misma frase. units.story:
A video claimed that a new study application had helped every participant double their test score. The caption linked to a company report, but the report described a smaller and more complicated result. Some participants improved, others remained at a similar level, and several had not completed the final test.

A student sharing the video initially focused on its confident presentation. She later noticed that the speaker was also selling access to the application. This did not automatically make every statement false, but it gave her a reason to inspect the evidence more carefully.

She compared the headline with the report's method and conclusion. The report measured performance on a particular set of exercises after a short trial. It did not assess whether learners could use the language spontaneously in another situation. The student posted a correction explaining this distinction and linked to the relevant section.

Some viewers complained that she was being unnecessarily negative. She replied that the application might still be useful; the problem was the certainty and breadth of the original claim. Evaluating a digital tool meant asking what had been tested and for whom, rather than choosing between complete enthusiasm and complete rejection.

units.model:
The advertisement for the new study platform claims that it guarantees fluent conversation after a short course. The demonstration shows several useful features, including audio practice and immediate feedback on fixed-answer exercises. These may help learners notice mistakes and review regularly.

However, the evidence presented does not support the guarantee. The examples show users answering familiar questions, not responding to unexpected information in a real conversation. The advertisement also does not explain how long the users practised or whether people with different starting levels achieved similar results.

I would consider the platform a possible practice tool rather than proof that a particular level has been reached. Before recommending it, I would want to test whether its activities help learners use the language in new situations and whether its feedback is accurate.

The company could make its message more convincing by describing the limits of the demonstration and publishing a clearer account of the evaluation. A useful tool does not need an unrealistic promise to be worth trying.

rules.title: Describir tendencias sin inventar causas
rules.text: Rise, fall, remain stable y fluctuate describen movimiento; sharply, gradually y slightly añaden grado. By indica cuánto cambia una cifra; to señala su valor final. From… to… fija inicio y final. Distingue percentage points de un cambio porcentual relativo. units.story:
A town tested closing one street to cars on Saturday mornings. Supporters expected a safer space for pedestrians and more visitors to local shops. Some shop owners worried that customers would find it difficult to collect large purchases. Residents with limited mobility also asked how they would reach nearby services.

During the first month, the number of people walking through the street increased. However, this coincided with a local festival, so the organisers could not attribute the entire rise to the closure. They collected comments and compared several ordinary Saturdays as well.

The trial was adjusted rather than simply extended unchanged. A collection point was created at one end of the street, and access arrangements were clarified for people who needed them. Signs were moved after visitors reported difficulty finding the alternative route.

At the review, the council described both benefits and remaining problems. The street felt more pleasant to many users, but deliveries still required coordination. The decision to continue the trial included a later review date and specific measures of access, footfall and business feedback. Treating the scheme as an experiment made it possible to improve the details without pretending that one rule would meet every need automatically.

Proposal: improving the waiting area

The purpose of this proposal is to make the space outside the community centre more comfortable and accessible. Visitors often wait there before activities, but the area has little shade and only one narrow bench.

One option would be to install a permanent shelter immediately. This could provide good protection, although it would require a larger budget and a careful review of the entrance layout. A second option is a temporary shade structure with two additional benches.

I recommend starting with the temporary arrangement for six weeks. It would be cheaper and could be adjusted if visitors found the position inconvenient. The main limitation is that temporary equipment would need regular checks and secure storage during unsuitable weather.

Volunteers should record how many people use the space at different times and collect brief comments about comfort and access. A clear path must remain available throughout the trial. During a visit to another city, Nina was invited to join a local group's evening meal. The message said to arrive "around seven." She reached the house at exactly seven and found the host still preparing the table. Nina wondered whether she had misunderstood the invitation and felt embarrassed about arriving too early.

The useful lesson was not a universal rule about punctuality. It was the value of clarifying expectations when words such as around, informal or join us leave room for interpretation. When Luis decided to improve his English, he designed an ambitious timetable with two hours of study every evening. For the first three days, he completed everything. A friend asked him to describe an ordinary busy day rather than an ideal one. Together they identified a shorter period that was usually available. Luis chose one practical task for each session, such as explaining a news item or responding to a recorded message. On quieter days, he could do more, but the basic plan did not depend on having unlimited energy or free time.

He also changed what he recorded. Instead of noting only whether he had followed the timetable, he wrote what he had practised and one difficulty to revisit. A missed day no longer erased the earlier work. The new routine was not a universal formula. It was an arrangement that better matched his circumstances and gave him information he could use to adjust the next session.

A film club asked members to write short reviews for people who had not seen the selected film. The first drafts contained enthusiastic adjectives but little explanation. One called the film amazing; another described it as boring. Neither helped a reader decide whether it matched their interests.

The organiser asked each reviewer to choose two criteria and support them with an example that did not reveal the ending. A member who disliked the slow pace acknowledged that the long conversations allowed the characters' relationships to develop. Another, who loved the visual style, admitted that the central mystery was easier to solve than expected.

The revised reviews did not become identical. Their disagreement became more informative. Readers could see whether the reviewer valued suspense, character development or visual atmosphere. The final recommendation could therefore address a particular audience instead of presenting personal taste as a universal judgement.

At the next meeting, members explained how one scene had shaped their interpretation. Discussing the evidence behind their reaction produced a richer conversation than voting on whether the film was simply good or bad.

units.story:
A customer wrote a long email after a workshop booking went wrong. The message described frustration in detail but did not include the booking date or explain what solution was wanted. The organiser replied asking for more information, which made the customer feel that the complaint had not been taken seriously.

A friend helped revise the email. They placed the booking reference and date in the first paragraph, explained the difference between the confirmed arrangement and what had happened, and requested either a replacement session or a refund. They removed several accusations about the organiser's motives because those could not be verified.

The revised version was shorter but more complete for its purpose. The organiser could identify the booking, investigate the problem and respond to a specific request. The customer did not need to hide the inconvenience; she explained its practical effect rather than repeating her anger.

The experience showed why good writing involves selecting information for a reader. Accuracy of grammar mattered, but it would not have solved the problem if the essential details and requested action had remained missing.

units.story:
Two learners prepared a discussion about organising a school event. Both memorised long statements containing impressive vocabulary. During the practice, each waited for the other to finish and then delivered the prepared statement. Their language was often accurate, but they barely responded to each other's ideas.

The teacher gave them a new task: choose one of three event plans while considering a limited budget and an accessibility requirement. Halfway through, she changed one condition. The learners could no longer rely entirely on their scripts. They had to ask questions, compare consequences and explain why a previous suggestion might need to change.

Afterwards, they listened to a recording and marked moments of successful cooperation: a useful follow-up question, a clear summary and a reformulation after a misunderstanding. They also noticed one place where both had spoken at once and missed an important condition.

For the second attempt, they prepared only brief notes and two ways to ask for clarification. The conversation still included pauses and mistakes, but it became more responsive. The improvement lay in using language together to reach a decision, not simply delivering a more polished speech.

units.story:
A learning group completed a course and wanted to know whether the progress charts reflected what they could do outside the exercises. Their tutor organised a project about improving a shared study space. Learners read two short proposals, listened to comments from fictional users and discussed a limited budget.

Each learner then wrote a recommendation for a different recipient. One addressed the centre manager, another wrote to students and a third explained the options to a visitor unfamiliar with the building. The facts were similar, but the selection of detail and register had to change.

The group compared first drafts with revised versions and identified where feedback had improved the message. They also repeated a discussion a week later with one new condition. Some expressions were easy to recognise but difficult to retrieve; some learners wrote clearly yet needed more practice responding to unexpected questions.

The final review did not reduce all this information to a single claim of perfect mastery. It produced a profile of strengths and next steps. Completing the course had given the learners material, practice and evidence. Continuing to use the language in new situations would determine how reliably those skills remained available.

units.case:
One learner obtained a high score in a reading quiz but struggled to explain the article to a partner. Another understood the main point orally but omitted an important condition when writing a summary. Their results were not contradictory: the tasks required related but different skills.

They chose separate follow-up activities. The first practised a short explanation from notes; the second compared summaries with the source to check conditions and qualifications. Both kept the earlier success in their records while addressing the new difficulty. Progress did not need to disappear because a harder task revealed another area to develop.

units.model:
Recommendation for the study centre

The centre is considering either extending its opening hours or improving the existing group-work room. Both options could benefit students, but they address different problems. The available feedback suggests that overcrowding during current hours is a more immediate concern than late access.

I therefore recommend testing a revised room layout before committing to longer opening times. Dividing the room into a quiet area and a clearly marked discussion area would help students choose a suitable place for their task. It would also require less additional staffing than keeping the whole building open later.

However, changing the layout would not automatically solve every problem. Noise might still travel between the two areas, and some students may genuinely need evening access. These concerns should be recorded during a six-week trial rather than dismissed.

The centre could monitor how each area is used and collect comments from both daytime and evening students. By the review date, staff would have clearer evidence about demand and practical difficulties. If the trial does not improve access to suitable study space, the longer-hours proposal should be reconsidered.

This recommendation is based on the limited feedback currently available. A wider consultation could change the balance between the two options.

pronunciation: Después de sonidos sordos distintos de /t/, -ed suele sonar /t/. No añadas una sílaba extra: watched tiene una sílaba.
Después de sonidos sonoros distintos de /d/, -ed suele sonar /d/, sin sílaba extra.
Tras /t/ o /d/, -ed añade una sílaba: wanted y needed tienen dos.
La -s puede sonar /s/ o /z/. En watches y changes aparece una sílaba adicional /ɪz/. Escucha y conserva la terminación.
/ɪ/ y /iː/ no se distinguen solo por duración: cambia también la posición de la lengua. Escucha palabras completas.
Las terminaciones -teen y -ty pueden confundirse. Escucha también la consonante final y confirma los números importantes.
I can come. · I cannot come.
Can suele reducirse cuando no lleva énfasis. No dependas solo de oír una /t/ final para identificar can’t: usa contexto y pide confirmación.
Could you repeat that? · Where do you live?
Escucha la frase por grupos y repite conservando el significado. La entonación varía con intención y acento; no hay una única melodía correcta.
Estos pares difieren por vocal y según el acento también por la /r/. Compara la voz británica y estadounidense disponible.
El acento principal cae al principio en estas palabras. Algunas sílabas débiles se reducen en el habla; busca claridad sin pronunciar todo con igual fuerza.
Destaca la información que corrige un malentendido. No pronuncies todo con la misma fuerza.
I said Tuesday, not Thursday morning.
La intención también se comunica mediante el ritmo, las pausas y el contexto. Las voces sintéticas no cubren toda la variación humana.
Practica despacio y luego dentro de una frase; conserva la claridad sin añadir una vocal entre cada consonante.
checklist: Contar una experiencia con una cronología clara y distinguir resultados, duración y hábitos.
Explicar previsiones y compromisos, negociar plazos y distinguir procesos futuros de resultados completados.
Analizar decisiones pasadas y sus consecuencias actuales sin confundir hechos con hipótesis.
Expresar deseos y desacuerdos con tacto, y convertir un arrepentimiento en una acción concreta.
Separar una deducción, una posibilidad y una crítica al explicar un hecho pasado.
Explicar procesos, informar de cambios y solicitar servicios usando pasiva y causativa.
Transmitir afirmaciones, preguntas y peticiones sin cambiar su intención ni confundir la fuente.
Añadir información relevante con relativas y participios, manteniendo claro a quién se refiere cada descripción.
Elegir gerundio o infinitivo según el verbo y explicar cómo cambia el significado.
Usar artículos, cuantificadores y concordancia para describir datos y recursos con precisión.
Comparar opciones usando criterios, grados y evidencia, sin confundir preferencia personal con superioridad universal.
Construir párrafos con contraste, causa, resultado y propósito, usando conectores adecuados a la estructura.
Ampliar vocabulario mediante familias, colocaciones y phrasal verbs, y recuperarlo en contexto.
Defender una opinión, reconocer incertidumbre y responder a objeciones sin exagerar la evidencia.
Comprender textos extensos, evaluar sus afirmaciones y resumir para otra persona sin copiar ni inventar datos.
Participar en reuniones, negociar responsabilidades y describir experiencia profesional con ejemplos concretos.
Comparar fuentes, identificar intención y debatir tecnología con afirmaciones proporcionadas.
Describir tendencias, comparar efectos y proponer acciones con ventajas, costes y condiciones.
Resolver malentendidos, pedir aclaraciones y comparar costumbres sin convertir experiencias individuales en reglas universales.
Hablar de hábitos y equilibrio personal, evaluar consejos y expresar recomendaciones sin prometer resultados universales.
Describir una obra, interpretar su efecto y escribir una reseña útil sin reducirla a me gusta o no me gusta.
Escribir mensajes con propósito, registro apropiado y peticiones concretas, y revisar su efecto en el lector.
Mantener un intercambio espontáneo, cooperar, aclarar y usar ritmo e entonación para comunicar sentido.
